topic: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 Review: Semantic Kernel + AutoGen Unified

key_points: Official 1.0 launch post positions Microsoft Agent Framework as production-ready for both .NET and Python, with stable APIs and long-term support.
Frames the product as the unified successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, combining enterprise features with multi-agent orchestration research.
Highlights stable orchestration patterns: sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic-One, with streaming, checkpointing, pause/resume, and human-in-the-loop support.

Notes preview areas around DevUI, Foundry Hosted Agent integration, Foundry observability/evaluations, AG-UI/CopilotKit/ChatKit adapters, skills, GitHub Copilot SDK, Claude Code SDK, and Agent Harness.
Strong writer takeaway: separate what is GA from what remains preview; readers need a practical migration and adoption lens, not just announcement coverage.
Official overview explains when to use agents versus workflows and explicitly advises using ordinary functions when a task can be handled deterministically.

Defines the framework as AutoGen-style simple agent abstractions plus Semantic Kernel enterprise features such as session state, type safety, middleware, telemetry, filters, and broad model/embedding support.
Introduces graph-based workflows for explicit multi-agent execution and robust state management for long-running and human-in-the-loop scenarios.
Includes important risk language for third-party systems, data sharing, non-Azure models, cost responsibility, and the need for custom responsible AI mitigations.
Strong writer takeaway: the best review angle is pragmatic boundaries: use MAF for controlled, production agent workflows, not every LLM feature.
Independent news coverage summarizes the 1.0 milestone and emphasizes stable APIs, long-term support, and the .NET/Python release.
Explains that Agent Framework consolidates prior Microsoft agent efforts into one open-source framework intended for both experimentation and enterprise deployment.
Clarifies project status: Microsoft positions MAF as the successor for new agent-development work; AutoGen is maintained for fixes/security, while Semantic Kernel remains active.
Lists stable areas: single-agent abstraction, service connectors, middleware hooks, agent memory/context providers, graph workflows, and multi-agent orchestration patterns.
Strong writer takeaway: use this as competitor framing for 'what changed' and 'what is safe to build on now.'
Build 2026 update says MAF reached 1.0 GA on April 2, 2026 and that new announcements build on the AutoGen/Semantic Kernel convergence.

Introduces Agent Harness as first-class production plumbing for shell/file access, human approvals, context management, memory, todo tracking, plan/execute modes, skills, background agents, web search, approvals, and OpenTelemetry.
Foundry Hosted Agents are positioned as the deployment path with managed identity, automatic scaling, persistent session state, isolation, observability, and versioning.
CodeAct is presented as an optimization for tool-heavy agents, reducing a representative workload from 27.81s/6,890 tokens to 13.23s/2,489 tokens.
Strong writer takeaway: the story has moved from 'unification' to 'operational agent runtime,' but some parts remain new enough to evaluate cautiously.
Competitor ecosystem guide compares seven agent frameworks and recommends Microsoft Agent Framework primarily for Microsoft-stack teams.
Positions MAF as the unified successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel with graph workflows, Azure AI Foundry responsible AI guardrails, and Python + .NET runtimes at 1.0 GA.
Frames agent framework choice around production reliability, observability, debugging, ecosystem integrations, and pricing transparency.
Strong writer takeaway: include a 'who should choose MAF vs LangGraph/OpenAI Agents SDK/CrewAI' section rather than reviewing it in a Microsoft-only vacuum.

stats.fact: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 was announced as production-ready for .NET and Python, with stable APIs and long-term support.
Microsoft's Build 2026 post states MAF reached 1.0 GA on April 2, 2026, after converging AutoGen and Semantic Kernel into one supported platform.
GitHub repository metadata checked on 2026-06-15: microsoft/agent-framework had 11,343 stars, 1,906 forks, 675 open issues, MIT license, and was pushed on 2026-06-14.

GitHub repository metadata checked on 2026-06-15: microsoft/autogen had 58,956 stars and 8,896 forks, but its README says AutoGen is now in maintenance mode and new users should start with Microsoft Agent Framework.
GitHub repository metadata checked on 2026-06-15: microsoft/semantic-kernel had 28,120 stars, 4,649 forks, 282 open issues, MIT license, and was pushed on 2026-06-12.

PyPI metadata checked on 2026-06-15: the agent-framework Python package latest version was 1.8.1, summary was 'Microsoft Agent Framework for building AI Agents with Python,' and it required Python >=3.10.
NuGet metadata checked on 2026-06-15: Microsoft.Agents.AI registration included recent versions 1.6.2, 1.7.0, 1.8.0, 1.9.0, and 1.10.0.
The Microsoft Learn overview says Agent Framework combines AutoGen abstractions with Semantic Kernel enterprise features and adds graph-based workflows for explicit orchestration.

The Microsoft Learn overview warns developers that third-party systems, non-Azure models, data sharing, costs, responsible AI mitigations, reliability, security, and compliance remain the application builder's responsibility.
Build 2026 CodeAct example reports a representative workload improving from 27.81 seconds and 6,890 tokens to 13.23 seconds and 2,489 tokens, a 52.4% time and 63.9% token improvement.

angles: The real product change is not just a rename: Microsoft is turning two overlapping projects into one supported runtime for production agent systems.
Best fit: .NET/Python teams already invested in Azure, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft.Extensions.AI, OpenTelemetry, MCP, or enterprise governance.

Key caution: 1.0 stabilizes the core, but many exciting pieces around Agent Harness, hosted agents, CodeAct, UI adapters, and deep Foundry integrations are new or preview-adjacent and need careful adoption.
Migration story matters: AutoGen users gain production lifecycle features; Semantic Kernel users gain simpler agent abstractions and richer multi-agent orchestration.
Competitive framing: MAF competes less as a quick prototype framework and more as a Microsoft-native alternative to LangGraph plus LangSmith-style production operations.
Unique insight: the docs' 'use a function if you can' guidance is valuable; MAF is strongest when autonomy, durable state, tools, and workflow coordination justify the complexity.
Reader pain point: developers want to know whether to start new projects on MAF, stay on Semantic Kernel, migrate AutoGen, or choose LangGraph/OpenAI Agents SDK instead.
AdSense/search angle: target high-intent migration and framework-comparison queries rather than broad AI-agent hype.
